fixes.answer: In my opinion, job satisfaction [[stems from]] more than just a good salary. Feeling that your work is meaningful and appreciated is [[paramount]]. A positive relationship with colleagues, opportunities to grow, and a sense of [[autonomy]] all contribute significantly. Ultimately, people are happiest when they feel valued and can see the genuine purpose behind what they do.
fixes.why: 'valued' and 'purpose' are plain; marked 'stems from' and 'paramount' (minimal rephrase)

fixes.answer: While money is obviously necessary, I believe that beyond a certain point, a sense of purpose matters more. A high salary provides comfort, but it does not [[compensate]] for feeling that your work is pointless. People who find meaning in their jobs tend to be far more engaged and resilient. So money is important up to a [[threshold]], but purpose provides the deeper, more lasting [[fulfilment]].
fixes.why: 'engaged' is plain; marked 'threshold'; softened the unsupported 'research suggests' claim

fixes.answer: The effects can be quite serious and far-reaching. Chronic dissatisfaction often leads to stress, low morale and even [[burnout]], which can spill over and harm a person's personal life and health. At work, it results in reduced productivity and higher [[staff turnover]]. Essentially, an unhappy workforce is [[detrimental]] to both the individuals involved and the organisation's overall performance.
fixes.why: 'productivity' and 'performance' are plain; marked 'burnout' and 'staff turnover'

fixes.answer: A job has a profound influence on overall wellbeing. Since we spend so many hours working, a fulfilling job can boost confidence and happiness that [[permeate]] our whole life. Conversely, a stressful or unfulfilling job can cause anxiety that affects our relationships and health. Work also shapes our identity and social status, so it is deeply [[intertwined]] with our [[sense of self]].
fixes.why: 'self' is plain; marked the phrase 'sense of self'

fixes.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. As automation takes over [[tedious]], repetitive tasks, workers may be freed to focus on more creative and meaningful work, which could boost satisfaction. There is also growing awareness of employee wellbeing. On the other hand, increased job insecurity and the pressure of constant [[connectivity]] could [[undermine]] satisfaction. So the outcome will likely depend on how wisely we manage these changes.

Employers can do a great deal. Offering fair pay and genuine [[recognition]] for good work is [[fundamental]]. Beyond that, providing opportunities for growth, some flexibility, and a supportive, respectful culture makes an enormous difference. Simply listening to employees and giving them a degree of autonomy over their work is powerful. Investing in staff wellbeing is not just ethical; it is genuinely [[profitable]] in the long run.
fixes.why: only 2 marks and 'autonomy' repeated from Q1; marked sir's 'recognition' and 'fundamental'

fixes.answer: Absolutely. A challenging job keeps you engaged and constantly learning, which prevents boredom and fuels personal growth. Overcoming difficulties also builds confidence and a real sense of accomplishment. The potential disadvantage is that if the challenge becomes overwhelming or [[unrelenting]], it can [[tip into]] stress and burnout. So the ideal is a job that [[stretches]] you without exhausting you.
fixes.why: 'exhausting' and 'overwhelming' are plain; marked 'unrelenting' and 'tip into'

fixes.answer: I do not entirely agree that it is a problem. Changing jobs frequently is often a sensible way to gain diverse experience, increase pay and find a better fit, especially in a fast-changing economy. The old model of [[lifelong loyalty]] is somewhat [[outdated]]. That said, changing too often can look unstable to employers and prevent one from developing deep [[expertise]], so a degree of balance is wise.
